Email: bduman@bartin.edu.tr Abstract The aim of the study is to examine the relations between higher education students' lateral thinking dispositions and inquiry skills. Survey design and Structural Equation Modelling were used in the study. The sampling of the study consisted of 975 prospective teachers attending three fac- ulties of education in three different state universities in Turkey. Inquiry Skills Scale and Lateral Thinking Disposition Scale were used to collect data. The collected data were analysed using R Studio programme. It was observed in the study that students' inquiry skills and lateral thinking dispositions were high. It was revealed in the study that inquiry skills predicted lateral thinking dispositions. Inquiry skills account for 31% of lateral thinking disposition. Thus, it can be concluded that lateral thinking dispositions of higher education students' depend on their inquiry skills at a percentage of 31%. Thus, it can be stated that the curricula are expected to pave the way for students to think through developing the thinking skills of individuals (Kurnaz, 2013, pp. 1–2). Thinking is an indispensable act in everyday life for all people. Human beings use the act of thinking intensively for many different purposes such as problem solving, understanding, building links, foreseeing, decision making, selection and comparison (Semerci et al., 2019). The way we think affects our plans, objectives and decisions. It seems difficult to make a compre- hensive definition of thinking as it is an abstract concept and has many dimensions. Therefore, it is not unusual to see differing definitions of thinking in literature. Halpern (1997, p. 3) describes thinking as “the process of creating new knowledge through prior knowledge”. Baron (2008) defines thinking as a high- level cognitive function used in the processes of making choices and judgements. It is a mental activity used to eliminate suspects on what to do, what to believe or what to pursue (Baron, 1993). Finally, Mayer (1983) indicates that thinking is a cognitive, goal- directed process and it can be observed in behaviour. Thus, the common characteristics of thinking observed in the above definitions are that it is a cognitive activity, it is used to make choices and create new knowledge and it is goal- directed. In educational contexts, thinking is usually defined as “a consciously goal- directed process, such as remember- ing, forming concepts, planning what to do and say, imagining situations, reasoning, solving problems, considering opinions, making decisions and judgments and generating new perspectives” (Moseley et al., 2005, p. 12). A great deal of research suggests that thinking should be taught in school (Brewerton, 2010; Burden, 1998; Csapo, 2001; Scheinin & Mehtalainen, 1999) as it is an integral part of learning. The need to teach thinking skills in schools has arisen due to societal demands, requirements of employment and sophisticated nature of everyday life (McTighe & Schollenberger, 1991). As Moseley et al. (2005, p. 9) emphasise, “thinking skills are needed, not only in the worlds of work, education and training but in the contexts of family, friendship and community and in the con- struction of personal and shared beliefs and values”. Also, students have been inevitably involved in the digital learning contexts for the past two years as a result of COVID- 19 pandemic, and digital learning has compelled stu- dents abruptly to develop skills of different types of thinking (Qi, 2021) that will be used fruitfully in the years to come. While giving the justifications for incorporating thinking skills, especially creative and lateral thinking, into educational processes, Kumari and Aggarwal (Kumari & Aggarwal, 2012, p. 32) indicate that “education system is so information oriented that it gives ready- made answers killing the natural tendency of students to explore, experiment and to experience”. They also complain that schools mainly focus on verbal, rational and time- based left hemisphere of the brain, neglecting the other. In addition, El Soufi and See (2019) indicate in their study that higher education students have lacked higher- order thinking skills especially for the past thirty years. However, research evidence demonstrates that attempts have been launched to foster higher- order thinking skills of higher education students through technology- based applications (Lu et al., 2021; Qi, 2021; Rababa, 2021; Varenina et al., 2021; Yulian, 2021). Thinking skills are studied under different sub- categories and some well- known ones are creative thinking, crit- ical thinking, reflective thinking, analytical thinking, convergent thinking, and divergent thinking. De Bono (1990) asserts that conventional thinking methods enable us to create fixed patterns of concepts and to improve and validate those patterns. However, we need more than conventional methods of thinking to create new patterns and restructure the existing ones, which frees us from the prevalence of outdated patterns of thinking. At this point, the term lateral thinking comes to the fore. Lateral thinking was originated by Edward de Bono in late 1960s to supplement creative thinking. It was put forward as a reaction to tightly structured or “standardised” way of thinking, which didn't allow for different or alternative perspectives. Edward de Bono is regarded by many as the leading international authority on teaching thinking, especially creative thinking. Lateral thinking can be considered as the extension of thinking skills by adding a new dimension. Waks (1997) regards the emergence of lateral thinking as a natural response to the “bombardment” of people in re- cent years with enormous amount of information. De Bono (1990) defines lateral thinking as skipping one pattern to another in an asymmetric model creatiDe oon system. While studying thinking skills, De Bono's main aim was to find the “sideways” to think creatively and to cease the judgmental or adversarial nature of habitual thinking patterns (Burgh, 2014). At this point, the phrase habitual thinking patterns mainly refers to two terms: vertical thinking, as de Bono calls it, and critical thinking. De Bono criticised sequential, logical or linear thinking, which he later called vertical thinking, along with critical thinking as he believed they would impede or hinder potential creative abilities of individuals. De Bono coined the term lateral thinking as a complementary equivalent of vertical thinking; and parallel thinking, which is cooperative and coordinated thinking, to replace critical thinking. Lateral thinking is needed when ordinary vertical thinking is unable to find a solution to a problem or when a new idea is required (De Bono, 2014) and it aims at “freeing the mind from the imprisonment caused by already established concepts and patterns” (Waks, 1997, p. 245). Chang and Zhou (2022) highlight this characteristic of the term stressing that lateral thinking depends on the indicators of imagination, perception and attention. With vertical thinking, one is confined to follow already- paved roads to go from A to B and it is almost impossible to find alternative routes or shortcuts; however, lateral thinking enables people to think alternatively and gain insight in the process of thinking. Thus, in addition to finding alternative ways to destination B, one can even change the destination as a result of lateral thinking. Therefore, it can be claimed that lateral thinking rejects any kind of boundaries or frameworks. Vertical thinking is a predictable and high- probability thinking that is employed by a large num- ber of people and it doesn't usually allow for the individual differences to emerge as much as lateral thinking does. However, lateral thinking enables people to exhibit their individual styles of thinking and problem- solving approaches. Thus, lateral thinking can be described as a way of thinking which requires breaking the habitual patterns of thinking, which were essentially employed by vertical thinking and eventually paves the way for creative thinking. De Bono does not make a distinction between vertical and lateral thinking with the aim of demonstrating which one is superior or inferior to the other. Rather, he emphasises the differences to use both terms effectively as both of them are necessary to think and produce alternative ways. He regards vertical thinking as the conven- tional way of thinking that everybody employs, whereas he considers lateral thinking as a way of thinking that aims at creating new patterns and restructuring the old ones to put forth mostly rare, unexpected or unusual thoughts. As De Bono (2014) maintains, lateral thinking is not a new, magic formula but simply a different and more creative way of using the mind. While using these two thinking skills for problem- solving, lateral thinking should precede traditional methods of vertical or logical thinking to have an effective output (Burgh, 2014) as confirmed by De Bono (1979, p. 12) stating that “there is no harm in rationalizing a vertical- thinking path to the solution after it has been reached by lateral thinking”. Lateral thinking is closely related to insight, creativity and humour (De Bono, 1977). These three constructs are usually God- given, whereas lateral thinking can be acquired later. As De Bono (1971, p. 13) indicates “it in- volves open- ended scanning techniques for generating options in the formative phases prior to decision selection, implementation and assessment”. What is more, “the skill of lateral thinking gives a person the opportunity to generate new ideas in the creative process” (Qi, 2021, p. 2). Lateral thinking could be used deliberately in cases like generating new ideas, problem solving, processing perceptual choice, periodic reassessment of assumptions, and prevention of sharp divisions and polarizations (De Bono, 1977; Elaldı, 2021). Thus, it can be asserted that lateral thinking is quite useful in urgent or troublesome cases. Having a clear idea about the theory of lateral thinking is not enough on its own as it is essential to put theory into practice to make it more substantial. In the related literature, it is frequently stressed to prefer lateral thinking over vertical thinking to make a difference as vertical thinking is used by lots of people and produces expected or predictable results. In order to arrange the ways used during lateral thinking for a better and more practical use of this type of thinking, some techniques have been introduced by de Bono. Major techniques are; generating alternatives, challenging assumptions, suspended judgement, fractionation, reversal method, brainstorming, anal- ogies, division, polarisation and random stimulation. De Bono (1977) states that the purpose of these techniques is to provide an opportunity for the practical use of lateral thinking so that one can gradually acquire the lateral thinking habit. Once the lateral thinking habit is acquired, some personal techniques can also be used as long as the principles of lateral thinking are followed. Researchers studied lateral thinking for different purposes. While some researchers (Karagöz, 2019; Lawrence & Xavier, 2013; Semerci, 2017; Yıldız & Yılmaz, 2020) just aimed at identifying the lateral thinking levels of higher education students with respect to some variables such as gender, department and seniority, some others studied the effect of lateral thinking skill on the development of English speaking skills (Nageswari et al., 2016), aca- demic achievement (Prakash & Vasimalairaja, 2021), creative thinking (Srikongchan et al., 2021), quality of instruc- tion in higher education (Selvam & Arasu, 2021; Ślaski & Grzelak, 2022), development of turnaround leadership and sustainable development goals of UN (Ghasemy et al., 2023) and group work (Elaldı, 2021). In addition, a group of researchers studied the relation between lateral thinking with intelligence and achievement (Kumari & Aggarwal, 2012), technology education (Waks, 1997), speaking competence (Omran & Krebet, 2022), social innovation (Aydemir, 2021), emphatical tendency (Arslan et al., 2022) and problem solving skills (Yazgan, 2021). More specifically, studies on mathematical lateral thinking were also observed (Julita & Herman, 2019; Nggaba et al., 2018; Susilawati et al., 2018). However, it could be claimed that the quantitative and qualitative research on lateral thinking conducted so far fails to appeal to the relation(s) lateral thinking has with inquiry (skills), which necessitates further relational research. Along with lateral thinking, the second variable focused on in this study is inquiry skills. Thinking and inquiry are the heart of cognitive skills (Güneş, 2012) and inquiry is essential to think (Yılmaz, 2019). Inquiry is a term in education and daily life that denotes seeking explanation or information by asking questions (Harlen, 2013). In addition, Martin- Hansen (2002, 35) points out that “inquiry includes the activities of students—such as posing questions, planning investigations, and reviewing what is already known in light of experimental evidence—that mirror what scientists do”. Moreover, inquiry requires using critical as well as logical thinking, considering alterna- tive explanations, and identifying assumptions (National Research Council, 1996). In essence, “inquiry is an active learning process in which students answer research questions through data analysis” (Bell et al., 2005). Inquiry skills, on the other hand, can be described as the skills which are required to dig beneath the ex- isting information or knowledge and which are one of the main sources for the implementation of other 21st century skills (Aslan, 2017). Inquiry skills are important in that they play a significant role in student learning and adapting to social life and life processes (Lim, 2001). It is noteworthy that higher- order mental processes are used in establishing an experience, individuals' discovering themselves, being curios and observant, and focusing on problem- solving while acquiring inquiry skills (Dow, 2000, p. 5). What is more, inquiry skills de- mand that students engage actively in collecting information, analysing findings and employing critical thinking concerning what is learned. Finally, using inquiry skills in the process of learning arouses curiosity, improves critical thinking, enhances student responsibility, encourages independent thinking and promotes reasoning skills (Honzel, 2012). A great deal of research indicates that research on inquiry learning mainly focuses on inquiry skills (Bailey, 2018; Bell et al., 2005; Gormally et al., 2009; Lim, 2001; Pedaste et al., 2015; Tornee et al., 2017). It is noteworthy that higher- order mental processes are employed in individuals' building an experience, exploring themselves, observ- ing, and focusing on problem solving (Dow, 2000, p. 5). Inquiry learning is usually defined as a process of exploring and it requires using a collection of skills that are essential in any aspect of life. Thus, inquiry skills are crucial with respect to adaptation to social life and vital processes (Lim, 2001). Individuals having inquiry thinking skills are able to employ scientific thinking processes and improve themselves in building knowledge through prioritising research and getting information (Lin, 2007). Inquiry learning helps individuals in the process of critical thinking and problem- solving in educational settings by encouraging questioning and checking the accuracy of newly ac- quired information. In this respect, it is quite important to incorporate inquiry skills more in curriculum studies with regards to supporting individuals' academic achievement as well as their cultural development. Therefore, integrating learning based on inquiry skills is necessary while identifying the syllabi of the courses (Bailey, 2018, p. 11). In the educational contexts based on inquiry thinking, the teacher guides students in the process and supports student learning based on experience with various case studies and explore themselves in learning- teaching process (Costa, 1991). In order to develop inquiry skills of students, it is necessary to evaluate the level of the skill in question in the supervision of teacher and to make use of different models in different learn- ing contexts (Davies et al., 2012). In the instructional processes where inquiry- based learning environments are encouraged, the necessity of identifying the shortcomings of instructors in inquiry skills and improving them is usually emphasised as the instructors are guides and leaders who play an active role in inquiry learn- ing (Lim, 2001). In inquiry learning environments, the guidance of teachers contributes to students' learning through inquiry thinking taking into account new ideas (Harrison, 2014). It is crucial for teachers to give prior- ity to real life implementations such as nature- environment education which enable students to be involved in studies with a critical viewpoint and to explore themselves while guiding students in learning environments that promote inquiry skills (Tornee et al., 2017). Given the important role of teachers in improving inquiry skills of students, their competence regarding inquiry skills during preservice training period gain greater im- portance. Thus, the higher the level of inquiry skills of teachers and prospective teachers are, the higher their competence in teaching inquiry skills to their students will be. When the related literature was reviewed, it was observed that prospective teachers' inquiry skills were ex- amined in some studies (Abalı Öztürk et al., 2017; Aldan Karademir & Saracaloğlu, 2017; Bedir & Duman, 2017; Dolapçıoğlu, 2020; Hayat & Rustaman, 2017; Katwijk et al., 2021; Şahin et al., 2017; Saputra et al., 2019; Yıldız Feyzioğlu, 2015). However, it was found out that the majority of the studies sought the relation between in- quiry skills and critical thinking skills, especially the effect of inquiry based learning on critical thinking (Al- afifi & Ambusaidi, 2014; Damopolii et al., 2021; Duran & Dökme, 2016; Ghaemi & Ghazi, 2017; Madhuri et al., 2012; Magnussen et al., 2000; Qing et al., 2010; Seranica et al., 2018; Wale & Bishaw, 2020). It was discovered that the relation between lateral thinking and inquiry skills of prospective teachers or of any other population has not been studied before. This was the main inspiration of the researchers involved in this study. Inquiry is related with critical thinking and lateral thinking is related with creative thinking. Thus, this study could be characterised as a study which investigates the relations between critical and creative thinking indirectly. Creativity and critical thinking are listed as the two main 21st century skills under the category learning and innovation skills (Partnership for 21st Century Skills, 2009) and 21st century skills are interconnected (Alkhayari, 2021; Myers, 2019). So, it is a good idea to study the relationship between lateral thinking, related with creativity, and inquiry, related with critical thinking. 2  | PU R P OS E O F TH E S T U DY This study examines the relationship between higher education students' inquiry skills and lateral thinking disposi- tions. To this end, answers for the following questions are sought: 1. What is the level of higher education students' inquiry skills and lateral thinking dispositions? 2. 6 of 22 |    DUMAN et al. 2.1 | Method 2.1.1 | Research design In the first stage, survey design was used to collect data. Data on higher education students' lateral thinking dis- positions and inquiry skills were collected through two scales and analysed using descriptive statistical methods. Creswell (2003) indicates that survey design provides researchers with a quantitative or numeric description of trends, attitudes, or opinions of a population, enabling them to make generalisations or draw inferences to the population. In the second stage, Structural Equation Modelling was employed in the study which “combines multiple regression, path analysis and factor analysis” (Fraenkel et al., 2012, p. 338). As MacLean and Gray (1998) point out “Structural Equation Modeling provides a statistically valid means of using the information we obtain through measurement to calibrate the relationships we hypothesise to exist between the underlying (latent) non- measurable variables”. What is more, it is one of the means that are employed in social sciences to evaluate the relations between or among variables and to test the theoretical models (Joreskog & Sörbom, 2001). A path analysis was conducted as the three sub- dimensions of inquiry skills were included in the correlational analysis in addition to main variables, lateral thinking disposition and inquiry skills. For Fraenkel, Wallen and Hyun (Fraenkel et al., 2012, p. 337), “path analysis is used to test the likelihood of a causal connection among three or more vari- ables”. Thus, a comprehensive analysis was carried out concerning the relations among the variables in the study. 2.1.2 | Study group The study group consisted of 975 higher education students attending the faculties of education of three state university in Turkey. The demographic data concerning the participants are given in Table 1. As seen in Table 1, 724 (74.3%) of the participants are female, whereas only 251 (25.7%) are male. That means the number of female participants almost triples that of male ones as most of the students at the faculties of edu- cation in Turkey consist of female students. It is a five- point Likert scale and con- sists of nine items and just one dimension. The KMO value of the scale was 0.794 and Barlett's test value was 1,585,363 (Df = 36, p = .000). The scale accounted for the 46.637% of the total variance. The factor loads of the scale ranged from 0.41 to 0.70 and item total correlations from .474 to .668. Test–retest correlation of the scale was .771 and the correlation coefficient between the two halves of the scale was .685. The Cronbach's Alpha coefficient of the scale was .75 and the same coefficient has been calculated for this study, the resulting figure is 0.78. Inquiry skills scale The Inquiry Skills Scale was developed by Aldan Karademir and Saracaloğlu (2013) and it is a five- point Likert scale consisting of fourteen items and three sub- dimensions. The sub- dimensions are information acquisition, in- formation control and self- confidence. All the items involved in the scale are positively worded. The KMO value of the scale was 0.854 and Barlett's test value was 1,513,582 (p < .01). The three factors in the scale accounted for the 51.98% of the total variance. The Cronbach's Alpha coefficients of the scale were .70 for information acquisi- tion,  .67 for information control, .90 for self- confidence and .79 for the overall scale. The Cronbach's Alpha coef- ficients calculated for each subdimension of this study were .70 for information acquisition, .67 for information control, .90 for self- confidence and finally .79 for the overall scale, respectively. 2.1.4 | Analysis of data In order to examine the predictory power of inquiry skills on lateral thinking through path analysis, analyses were conducted for missing and extreme values. When the data set was investigated, it was observed that there were no missing values. Data belonging to 24 participants were extreme values.
